doc.title: Michael Moore interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: The Whitney Balliett 'greatest living bassist' quote
summary: Moore says the Balliett line was a blessing and a curse that made enemies; it was later removed from the book, though he has used it in publicity.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: We are filming this afternoon for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive in Chautauqua, New York, and I am very pleased to welcome Michael Moore, who Whitney Balliett called “the greatest living bassist.” Did you see that quote?

Did I see it — I did one whole room in that article. Well, yeah, I did. Actually it was nice to read but it was tough to live with because I mean I didn’t agree, and it’s the kind of thing that made a lot of enemies. People I didn’t even know would come up to me and say, like I wrote it.
Yeah, you know, that kind of thing. It was a blessing and a curse.
I think it’s impossible to say that one person is the greatest living something, because there’s so many parameters involved.

Of course. It’s not a high jump contest. And I think at the time he had quite carte blanche at the magazine to say whatever he wanted. And I know in later books the editor made him take that first line out, which I agreed with. I think that when he actually went to the editor to publish the book they made him take that out. And so I mean the article was fine without it. It was actually much easier on me and everybody else. But by that time the damage or whatever, had been done.
Right. It will show up for a while in programs, much like it did here.
Right, of course. And I must say I’ve used it myself in my publicity.
